name: Media Optimizer
description: Inspect any media file from inside Jellyfin and convert it with FFmpeg: resolution, codec, bit depth, bitrate and audio presets, plus a genuinely lossless mode whose bit-exactness is verified by hash after every encode. Conversions run in a background queue and the original file is never modified until the result passes verification.
overview: Inspect and convert media files from inside the Jellyfin interface.

versions.changelog:
- New: moving media between drives, from Dashboard -> Move Media. It lists every library folder
with how full its drive is and how much of the library lives there, moves individual files or
a whole folder onto another drive, and says what would happen before anything does: how many
files, how much data, what would be left free and which files would be skipped and why.
- A move is a separate action from a conversion, with its own queue and its own history:
nothing is re-encoded and not a byte of the file changes. "Move to another drive..." is a
separate entry in the 3-dot menu for administrators.
- Each file is copied to a hidden staging name on the destination drive, checked against the
original by size and by hash, and only then renamed into place and the original deleted. A
failure or a cancellation before that leaves the library exactly as it was, and an original
that cannot be deleted takes the copy away again rather than leaving a duplicate. Within one
drive the file is renamed instead, which is instant.
- Artwork, .nfo files and external subtitles travel with the media file, the library entry is
repointed rather than rescanned so watched state and playlists survive, the folder layout
below the library folder is preserved, and an emptied folder is cleaned up.
- Moves pause while anyone is streaming, and a file someone is watching is never moved. The
housekeeping task now also clears partial copies left behind by a server that stopped
mid-move.

- New: a rule can be confined to one library, so "convert the TV recordings, never touch the
films" is something you can actually say.
- New: the concurrency limit is now counted in ordinary conversions rather than in jobs. A 4K
encode counts as two, because two of them at once is not twice the work, it is a server that
stops answering. A smaller job still runs in the room a large one leaves.
- New: "Measure it" in the conversion dialog. Every other number shown before a conversion is
modelled; this one encodes three short stretches of the real file with the real settings and
reports what they actually produced, including how much the samples varied and how long the
whole thing would take at the speed they ran.
- New: it also measures how much worse it will look. The samples are compared with the source
frame by frame — VMAF where FFmpeg has it, SSIM otherwise — and the answer is given both as a
score and in words, so "how much quality am I losing?" stops being answered with a preset name.
- Fixed the last line of FFmpeg's output occasionally going missing, which is the line carrying
the error, the hash or the score. It cost about one run in twenty-five.
- New: the dashboard file list now ranks the library by what there is to gain rather than by
size, and says where the saving would come from. The biggest file in most libraries is a remux
that is already efficiently encoded.
- New: finished and failed conversions are written to Jellyfin's activity feed, with what the
file went from and to, how much was freed, and until when the original can be put back.
- New: automatic rules. A rule says which files it takes — films or episodes, resolution, size,
container, codec, whether anyone has watched it, how long it has been in the library — and what
to do with them, and a nightly task applies it. Every rule has a ceiling on how many files it
may queue in one run and a minimum saving below which it leaves a file alone; a new rule is
saved switched off, and "Preview" says exactly what it would take, and why it passed over the
rest, without queueing anything.
- Fixed a bit-exact conversion being failed and thrown away. The hash comparison paired the Nth
lossless track with the Nth audio track of the output, which is only the same track when
nothing in front of it was merely copied — so a file with a copied commentary ahead of its
lossless track compared two different tracks and reported a mismatch.
- Fixed nightly housekeeping being able to delete the output of a job that was still running.
The job id in the working file's name is what marks it as in use, and it was being read with a
rule that never matched.
- Fixed a lossless HDR encode quietly not being lossless. FFmpeg keeps only the last occurrence
of an option, and the encoder parameters were being passed twice — once for lossless, once for
the HDR signalling. Hardware encodes had the same problem with the encoder preset, making the
chosen speed a coin toss.
- Fixed "disk reclaimed" reading zero for conversions that replaced and deleted the original —
the one setting that frees the space immediately.
- Pausing the queue now survives a restart. It was held in memory, so a restart — the thing that
follows every upgrade — resumed encoding without telling anyone.
- 10-bit files are now recognised as 10-bit even when the container does not say so, instead of
defaulting the conversion to 8-bit and losing a bit of picture nobody agreed to lose.
- Settings that cannot work are now refused with a sentence naming the setting, rather than
reaching FFmpeg and coming back as an error about a flag nobody typed.
- Every conversion now gives the muxer enough room to interleave streams whose timestamps drift
apart, which was otherwise a job that failed hours in.
- The conversion dialog no longer keeps polling the server after it is closed, can be driven from
the keyboard, and the dashboard no longer stacks up duplicate button handlers when you navigate
back to it.
- Security: removed an endpoint that accepted a document from anyone and returned it as HTML.
Endpoints that reveal where files live on the server, list the queue, or make the server read a
whole media file now require an administrator, and the file information dialog no longer tells
a non-administrator the absolute path of the file on the server.
- Fixed nightly housekeeping deleting every file in the working directory older than six hours,
rather than only the ones this plugin wrote. If you pointed the working directory at a folder
that already had something else in it, that something else was being deleted.
- A conversion that has to copy its output to another disk no longer risks leaving a full-size
partial copy next to your media forever if the server loses power mid-copy.
- New: "Find the setting" in the conversion dialog. Instead of reporting what a quality setting
does, it finds the setting: say how close to the source the result has to look —
indistinguishable, very hard to tell apart, or slightly softer — and the server encodes short
stretches at several settings and picks the smallest file that still measures up on this file.
Every "use CRF 22" is a number that suited somebody else's files; a grainy film and a flat
animated series want settings four or five apart. It confirms its answer at three points across
the film, where the worst of the three has to meet the target, and says plainly when a source
cannot reach one at all.
- A job interrupted by the server stopping is no longer resumed for ever. If a file or a setting
is what takes the server down mid-encode, requeueing it on every boot makes the plugin the
cause of a reboot loop; after three interruptions the job is held with a note saying what to
try instead, and you can still run it by hand.
- Every number in the conversion dialog now says what kind of number it is. A prediction made
without the file's own bitrate is labelled a rough guess, and a file nothing can be predicted
from says so, instead of both being shown exactly as confidently as a measurement.
- The setting for measuring picture quality alongside size now has a control on the settings
page. It was added with the measurement itself and left off, so only somebody willing to edit
the plugin's XML by hand could turn it off.
- Enabling HEVC or AV1 encoding in Jellyfin's own transcoding settings now takes effect without
restarting the server, and a corrected FFmpeg path is picked up the same way.
- Fixed two people using the conversion dialog at the same time being able to see each other's
permissions.
- Fixed a lossy DTS-ES Matrix track being read as lossless DTS-HD MA, which had the plugin
calling a conversion of it bit-exact and predicting a file several times smaller than it
would be.
- Fixed the one conversion failure the checks could not see: an output missing a track. An
encoder or muxer that drops a track it could not write and still reports success produces a
file that parses and runs for exactly the right length — and the next step replaces your only
copy with it. The plan now records what it maps and verification counts what came out, so a
conversion that lost an audio or subtitle track is refused with the track named, and the
original is left alone.
- New: tell it what the footage is. Grain and animation want opposite decisions from an encoder,
and it is the one thing about a file you can see instantly and no probe can tell reliably, so
"Content" in the dialog — live action, animation, film grain — is passed straight through to
the encoder's own tuning. Line art stops being smoothed; grain is kept rather than smeared
into blotches. Offered only for the x264 and x265 encoders, which are the ones that have it,
and a rule can carry it too — which is where it fits best, since a rule already narrows a
library down.
- Measuring and searching no longer hold the connection open while they work. A minute is
longer than most reverse proxies will wait, so both now run on the server and the dialog asks
how they are going — and closing the dialog stops the encoding instead of leaving it running.
- Opening the conversion dialog on a file that is already converting now shows that conversion,
with its progress and a way to cancel it, instead of a form the server would refuse. The
dashboard's file list offers "Show progress" for those rows rather than a greyed-out "Queued".
- New: "Preview tonight's run" — what every switched-on rule would take, in one answer, with
each file saying which rule would take it. Previewing one rule at a time only ever answered
what that rule does.
- Rules can be reordered. They are applied top to bottom and the first one to take a file keeps
it, so with two rules that overlap, which one is above decides which converts the file — and
there was no way to change it. Every job a rule queues now says which rule queued it.
- A failed save on the settings page now says so. It did nothing at all: the loading overlay
stayed up, no message appeared, and the settings were the old ones — so a page whose save had
failed looked exactly like one whose save had worked. Settings that cannot be read now say
that too, and warn you not to save a form that is showing its defaults over them.
- The totals and the conversion queue on the Conversions page now say when they could not be
read. A failed request and an empty queue looked identical, on the one page somebody opens to
check whether last night's conversions actually ran.
- The conversion progress view now says when it has lost contact with the server instead of
leaving the bar where it stopped. "Encoding — 43%" that has quietly stopped updating is not a
stale number, it is a sentence that is no longer true, and it is what somebody reads when
deciding whether to wait up for a conversion. The conversion itself is unaffected, and the
message goes away when the server answers again.
- New: the finished conversion is measured against the original. Everything else here measures
a conversion before it happens, from short samples; this compares three stretches of the
finished file with the same moments of the original and records what it found, so the job
history and the activity feed say what the conversion actually cost rather than what was
predicted. It also makes a promise possible: "refuse a conversion that measures worse than…"
fails the job instead of replacing your original, and your file is left exactly as it was.
Off by default. A conversion that copied the video, or one verified bit-exact by hash, is not
measured — it cannot have changed the picture.
- A cancel the server refuses now says so, in the dialog and on the dashboard. "Cancel
conversion" greyed out its own button and said nothing, so a refused cancel looked exactly
like an accepted one while the encode carried on — and on the dashboard, "run the rules now",
"cancel everything pending" and "free up space" all discarded whatever the server said.
Saying no to the confirmation is still silent; a failure names what did not happen.

- Fixed the dialog showing a file as having no video and no audio, with a blank duration and
bitrate, and still offering to convert it. FFprobe's answer was only ever used to fill in
details on top of Jellyfin's own stream data; if Jellyfin had no record of the file, that
answer was discarded and the dialog described the file as empty. FFprobe now supplies the
whole track list when Jellyfin has nothing, and the item's own media source is tried before
either of them.
- A file whose contents genuinely cannot be read is now refused with the reason, instead of
offering "Start conversion" on a job that would map no streams and write an empty file.
- Fixed MP4 being offered for a TrueHD or Atmos remux. The container check needs the audio
track list to know MP4 cannot hold it, so with no stream data it silently passed and the
job died at the muxer.
- Dropdowns no longer cut their own labels off mid-sentence on a phone. A select clips rather
than wraps, so the labels are short now and the explanation sits underneath where it can wrap.

- Fixed the Codec dropdown being empty and every conversion being rejected with "No video
encoder was selected". When the plugin could not read FFmpeg's encoder listing it was left
with no codecs at all, and that empty result was then cached until the server was restarted.
A probe that finds nothing is no longer kept, the listing is parsed in a way that survives
FFmpeg adding a column, and FFmpeg is asked about each encoder individually as a last resort.
- The dialog now says why nothing can be re-encoded, naming the actual FFmpeg problem, instead
of showing an empty Codec dropdown and defaulting Video to "Keep exactly as it is".
- Fixed the chosen codec not reaching the server. A dropdown showing its first entry was not
the same as that entry having been selected, so a conversion could be rejected for having no
encoder while the form plainly showed one.
- A codec this server no longer provides is shown as such in the dropdown rather than being
silently swapped for a different one.

- "Try again" now works on jobs that failed before 1.4.1.0. A queued job carries the settings it
was created with, so retrying one simply replayed the container that could not hold the file.
The container is now re-checked every time a job runs, so a stale job is corrected rather than
failing the same way twice.
- Failure messages now lead with the line that names the cause. FFmpeg prints it first and then
floods its output with thread teardown, so the previous message kept the last 500 characters
and cut off the only useful sentence.
- Failures record which version of the plugin produced them.

- Fixed conversions to MP4 failing immediately on any file with text subtitles. The plan copied
the source subtitle track into MP4, which has no format for it, so FFmpeg refused to write the
file and the job died having encoded nothing. Text subtitles are now converted to MP4's own
subtitle format, and left untouched in MKV.
- Fixed MP4 being chosen for files carrying TrueHD, Blu-ray PCM or other audio MP4 cannot store.
Those now stay MKV so the track is kept exactly as it is, and the reason is shown in the dialog
instead of the container silently changing.
- Every job now runs half a second of the real encode through the real muxer before starting.
Anything FFmpeg would reject fails in a second with a readable message, rather than after hours
of encoding.
- Image-based subtitle detection now recognises DVB and XSUB tracks as well as PGS and DVD.

- Much faster, without touching the encoder. Replaced originals are now renamed in place
instead of copied to a data folder, encoding writes into the media folder so the finished
file is moved by rename, and the full decode verification that doubled every job is off by
default. On a 5 GB film that is minutes of pure disk copying removed per job.
- Hardware encoding is now tuned for quality — multi-pass, lookahead, B-frames and adaptive
quantisation — landing 10-20% larger than a slow CPU encode rather than 50%.
- New: replace and delete the original immediately, or replace and keep it for a set number of
days. Every replacement is written to replacements.log.
- Finished jobs are removed automatically after 30 days.
- The dashboard is tidier: status collapses to one line, the file picker and the history are
dropdowns, and running jobs are separated from finished ones.
- Process priority is no longer lowered by default, which was quietly slowing every encode.

- Keep only the audio and subtitle languages you actually use; everything else is removed.
This is bit-exact for the tracks you keep and is often the largest saving available. A file
is never left with no audio at all.
- Optionally remove commentary and audio-description tracks.
- The queue is now crash-safe: every change is written to disk before it is acknowledged, and
an encode interrupted by a restart or a power cut is picked up again automatically.
- Speed settings: fastest / balanced / smallest file, and a switch to use the graphics card,
which is typically ten to twenty times faster than the CPU.
- A status panel entry that measures this server's real encoding speed and names what is
slowing it down.
- Statistics: disk actually reclaimed, average reduction, and how much is still held for undo.
- Pause the queue, run a job next, cancel everything pending, and free the space held by
originals awaiting undo.
- Scrub previews are rebuilt after a file is replaced, instead of staying stale.

- Fixed the dialog's two panes rendering on top of each other. It now lives in a shadow root,
so no stylesheet on the page can reposition it.
- Fixed every default predicting a bigger file. Size is now estimated from the source's own
bitrate, and a container that mis-tags the video stream no longer skews it.
- New presets: Standard (better codec), Medium (one resolution step down), High reduction
(a step down plus a lower bitrate). The dialog opens on whichever actually helps the file.
- Removed the invented encode time. A real one appears once the server has measured itself.
- Subtitle warnings are collapsed into one line with a "Use MKV instead" button.
- Select several files on the dashboard and convert them all with one preset.
- Sort and filter the dashboard list by size, resolution, bitrate, watched state, container
and codec.
- MP4 and Replace are now the defaults; files whose subtitles MP4 cannot carry stay MKV.
- Reworded the options that were unclear.

- Conversions can now be started from the dashboard page, so the plugin is fully usable
without the in-app buttons.
- Fixed the in-app buttons never appearing: File Transformation 2.5 added admin auth to its
HTTP registration endpoint, so registration now goes through its in-process service instead.
- Added a status panel that reports each part of the plugin separately.
